body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Nurse staffing and missed nursing care in 32 hospitals: a cross-sectional survey of registered nurses","authors":"Oyelaran-Strand P, Kowalczyk-Ade M, Haddad-Lindgren S","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Hospital Nursing Workforce","doi":"10.5555/jhnw.2019.0233","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We surveyed 1,410 registered nurses on medical and surgical units in 32 hospitals using a 22-item missed-care checklist about the last shift worked. At least one activity was left undone on the last shift by 71 percent of nurses, most often comfort talk, mouth care and patient teaching. Each additional patient per registered nurse was associated with higher odds of reporting missed care (odds ratio 1.09, 95 percent CI 1.04 to 1.14). Units with more licensed practical nurses in the skill mix reported more missed teaching and discharge preparation. Staffing was reported by the nurses themselves, and the response rate was 38 percent."},{"title":"Missed care on medical and surgical wards: results of a union-led member survey","authors":"Western Nurses Association research committee","year":null,"venue":"Association member report series","providerType":"report","abstract":"An online survey of 2,960 members working on medical and surgical wards asked about care left undone on the most recent shift. Sixty-eight percent reported at least one missed activity, and 41 percent reported a missed or late timed medicine. Respondents described short staffing, unplanned admissions and sick calls as the main reasons. The report gives no response rate and no information on how the survey was distributed, and its publication date is not stated anywhere in the document. Free-text comments describe night shifts as the hardest to cover."},{"title":"Shift-level staffing shortfalls and missed care: linking nurse reports to scheduling records","authors":"Brandt-Achebe L, Morales-Okoro J, Svensson-Iqbal R","year":2022,"venue":"Nursing Workforce Analytics","doi":"10.5555/nwa.2022.0145","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Nurses on 12 units reported missed care at the end of 2,870 shifts over six months, and each report was linked to planned and actual nursing hours from the scheduling system. Missed care was reported after 44 percent of shifts that ran at least 10 percent below planned hours and after 27 percent of shifts at or above plan. The difference persisted after adjustment for the unit's mean acuity score. Night shifts had fewer reports overall but a steeper increase with shortfall. Linking reports to the actual shift avoided relying on nurses' recall of their staffing."},{"title":"Instruments for measuring missed nursing care: a systematic review of measurement properties","authors":"Nakamura-Fitch E, Obi-Castellanos R, Petit-Wanjiru D","year":2020,"venue":"International Review of Nursing Measurement","doi":"10.5555/irnm.2020.0077","providerType":"review","abstract":"We identified 14 instruments that measure missed or unfinished nursing care. Internal consistency was reported for 12 and test-retest reliability for 5. Construct validity was supported for 6 instruments, mostly by correlations with staffing. Instruments differed in recall period, from the last shift to the last month, and in whether they asked about the reasons for missed care. A last-shift recall period and a separate reasons section were recommended to reduce recall bias and to separate what was missed from why. None of the instruments had been validated for licensed practical nurses."},{"title":"Patient acuity, staffing and missed care: accounting for acuity weakens the association","authors":"Lindqvist-Oduya A, Ferreira-Nwosu K","year":null,"venue":"Nursing research meeting abstract book","providerType":"conference-abstract","abstract":"In this conference abstract, 640 nurses on 20 units reported missed care for their last shift, and unit staffing was measured as patients per nurse. Unadjusted, each additional patient per nurse was associated with more missed care (odds ratio 1.11). After adjustment for the mean acuity score of the unit on the survey day, the association was no longer clear (odds ratio 1.03, 95 percent CI 0.97 to 1.10). The authors suggest that staffing ratios already reflect acuity in units that staff to acuity. Methods are described briefly and the year of the meeting is not given."},{"title":"Improving response to hospital nurse surveys: protected time versus reminders","authors":"Halvorsen-Mbeki T, Dubois-Achterberg N","year":2017,"venue":"Survey Methods in Health Workforce Research","doi":"10.5555/smhwr.2017.0019","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across 16 units in two hospitals, we compared a web survey with three email reminders against the same survey completed during 20 minutes of protected paid time. Response was 31 percent with reminders and 52 percent with protected time. Responders under reminders were more often day-shift and full-time nurses, whereas protected time narrowed the difference between day and night shifts. Item nonresponse was similar in both arms. Protected time cost about 9 nursing hours per 100 responses, which the hospitals judged affordable for an annual survey."},{"title":"Missed nursing care and patient-reported experience on medical units","authors":"Achebe-Sorensen F, Varga-Tanaka I, Reid-Mensah O","year":2024,"venue":"Patient Experience in Hospital Care","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We matched unit-level missed care rates from a nurse survey with patient experience scores from 3,400 discharged patients on 26 medical units. Units where nurses more often reported missed comfort talk and teaching had lower patient ratings of being told about new medicines and of help with pain. The association with overall ratings was weak. Patient experience surveys were returned by 29 percent of discharged patients, so the matched units differ in who answered. Unit-level aggregation cannot show which patients received less care."}]}
